job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Jade Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet. I get up early out of habit, walk the dog, Biscuit, round the reservoir in Hallbeck, and then I'm at the kitchen table by nine with the job sites open. I apply for maybe three roles a day, then I stop, because I read once that sending too many makes you sloppy. In the evening I have dinner with my parents and my grandfather, and we watch the news.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what did your internship involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marketing and business administration, a good result. I did five weeks at a furniture retailer's marketing office, where I updated the product listings and did the monthly sales report in a spreadsheet. They liked my reports, but there was no job at the end of it. I don't use AI tools, and I don't plan to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, the fuss was overdone. At home I'd say what I always say, which is that most new things turn out smaller than the headlines. I wouldn't post anything online, I don't like having opinions on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it means the job market stays tough for the usual reasons. There are plenty of openings, but everyone wants someone with two years of experience, and I have five weeks. And some routine reporting does get automated, which was half of my internship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my routine going: three applications a day, a call every week to the furniture retailer's manager Ms Orlov in case something opens, and a visit to the university careers office. I'd also ask my dad if his firm needs a junior admin, even though I don't want to work for family. I wouldn't change anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a little tense. Nothing is going wrong, and I still feel behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you want to work at your dad's firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why don't you want to work for your dad's firm?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does feeling behind mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd never know if I got the job or just got a favour. I want to earn a job somewhere I'm not anybody's daughter. That might be pride, I admit, and pride doesn't pay rent.

say: I'd say the fuss was **overdone**, as most new things turn out smaller than the headlines.
think: The market stays tough for usual reasons: everyone wants **two years** of experience and I have five weeks.
Routine reporting still gets automated, which was half my internship.
do: Keep my routine of **three applications** a day.
Call Ms Orlov, the retail marketing manager, every week in case a post opens.
feel: **Tense** but fine: nothing is wrong, yet I feel behind.
S0.quote: I want to earn a job somewhere I'm not anybody's daughter.
fieldNote: Her resistance to change shows as **routine**, not panic.
Refuses a family job out of pride, which she recognises.
Feels behind peers, though her cushion is strong.

steps.text: Send three job applications every day
Phone Ms Orlov at the furniture retailer every week
Book a session at the university careers office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what people expected and what firms wanted, and it'll cost some jobs. At work I'd say let's see how it's rolled out before judging. I'd tell my friends I'd rather see the results than argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Marketing reporting, product listings, the social media posts, those are the tasks software does now. The entry jobs for my degree are mostly those tasks, so there'd be fewer of them, and I'm not good at jumping on new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for a job in a place where the work is hard to automate: a retailer's buying team, a charity or a small manufacturer where people talk to each other. I'd ask my friend Leni to show me an AI tool once, in person, but I wouldn't use it by myself. And I'd extend my savings by cutting what I spend on going out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit annoyed. I didn't ask for this, and I'm expected to move at someone else's speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it easier for you to pick up a new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make it easier for you to pick up a tool?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd cut going out. How much would that save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone patient, a small group, and a real task rather than a demo. I learn a new tool by doing it three times with a person next to me. Once I've done that, I'm fine, but I don't enjoy the first week.

say: I'd say it was what **firms wanted** and will cost some jobs.
I'd rather see results than argue.
think: Reporting, listings and social posts are what software does now, so **fewer entry jobs** exist for my degree.
I'm not good at jumping on new tools.
do: Look for jobs hard to automate: a **buying team**, a charity or a small manufacturer.
Ask my friend Leni to show me an AI tool once, in person.
Cut spending on going out to stretch my **savings**.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit annoyed at moving at someone else's speed.
S1.quote: I learn a new tool by doing it three times with a person next to me.
fieldNote: Knows exactly **how she learns**, which makes her resistance practical.
Her fear targets the specific tasks she did on her internship.
Looks for work where people talk to each other.

steps.text: Apply to retailer buying teams and small manufacturers
Ask my friend Leni to show me an AI tool in person
Cut going-out spending to stretch my savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is crazy, and somebody should slow it down. At the kitchen table I'd say my grandfather's generation saw factories change over decades, and we'd get two years. I'd write to my local politician, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. My degree is built on tasks software does well. Everyone my age would be competing for the few jobs left, and I'm the one who still doesn't use the tools. I'd go from behind to a long way behind in a single step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to anything with a person at the centre, such as a hospital reception, a school office, a bank counter, and I'd take a lower salary to get in. I'd also ask my dad about a trade course, like surveying, since he's in that world. And I'd cut spending hard and keep savings for at least a year of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd feel like the music stopped and everyone found a chair except me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd write to a politician. What would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd write to a politician. What would you say?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move into a trade like surveying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That someone needs to make the companies hire and train people before they swap them for software. Just a simple letter, not angry. I'd want a reply, even a bad one, to know someone is actually thinking about it.

say: I'd say two years is **crazy** and somebody should slow it down.
I'd write to my local politician for the first time.
think: My degree is built on tasks software does well, and I still **don't use the tools**.
I'd go from behind to a long way behind.
do: Apply for jobs with a **person at the centre**, like hospital reception or a bank counter.
Ask my dad about a trade course such as **surveying**.
Cut spending hard to keep a year of rent.
feel: **Scared**, like the music stopped and everyone found a chair except me.
S2.quote: I'd feel like the music stopped and everyone found a chair except me.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** turns from preference into fear in this version.
She considers a trade, which she has never mentioned before.
Takes an unfamiliar step: writing to a politician.

steps.text: Apply for hospital reception and bank counter jobs
Ask my dad about a surveying course
Cut spending to keep a year of rent
Write to my local politician about training and hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's better than two years, but not by much. I'd tell people to start preparing and stop pretending it's a long way off. I'd say we need courses in towns like Hallbeck, not only in the capital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still be afraid. Five years is long enough to hope, and short enough that I can't pretend I'll catch up by waiting. If I don't have a job in a year, I'd be 24 and competing with every graduate who can do twice what I can with a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd accept a job fast, even if it's dull, and do it well so I have a reference. In the evenings I'd take an AI course through the library, in a group, once a week. I'd also save as much as I can, because I think I'll need money for a change. And I'd stay at home until I've saved the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Worse than the slow one, better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really commit to a group course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you really commit to a course in a group?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of job would you take quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it's weekly and somebody's expecting me. I stick to routines, so if the course is a routine, I'll follow it for five years. It's why I walk the dog every morning, nobody has to remind me.

say: I'd say five years is better than two but **not by much**, and towns like Hallbeck need courses.
I'd tell people to stop pretending it's far off.
think: Five years is long enough to hope and short enough that I can't just **wait**.
If I'm jobless at 24, I'd compete with graduates who do twice as much.
do: Accept a **dull job fast** and do it well for a reference.
Take a weekly **AI course** at the library, in a group.
Save hard and stay at home until the deposit is saved.
feel: **Heavy**: worse than the slow picture, better than the fast one.
S3.quote: I stick to routines, so if the course is a routine, I'll follow it for five years.
fieldNote: Turns her love of **routine** into a plan for learning.
Believes she must work fast now to avoid being overtaken.
Still carries a sense of heaviness and delay.

steps.text: Accept the first reasonable job and build a reference
Join a weekly group AI course at the library
Save most of my pay for a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years sounds like plenty, but plenty is the thing people waste. I'd tell my friends not to treat it as someone else's problem. I'd also say towns should plan what happens to people who lose office jobs, because it will take them by surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel a bit calmer, but not safe. In ten years I could grow into a senior role, and people who can talk to customers and handle the numbers should do all right. What I don't want is to find out at 31 that I stayed in the same place the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job in the next year, aim for a team that has an AI tool already, and learn it from colleagues who know it. I'd save for a flat by 27. I'd also take one professional course, maybe in project management or finance, to move beyond the entry-level jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. It's the one picture where I can see my own life in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good version of the next ten years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would a good version of the next ten years look like?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd most want to be different from today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small flat, a team I like, and a boss who explains things. I want a small, solid, reliable life, earning enough to help my parents when they're older. That's honestly all of it.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, but **plenty gets wasted**.
I'd tell friends it isn't someone else's problem.
think: I'd feel calmer but not safe: customer-facing and numbers skills should do **all right**.
I fear staying in the same place at 31.
do: Get a first job within a year, in a team already using an **AI tool**.
Take one **professional course** to move beyond entry level.
feel: **Steadier**: the one picture where I see my own life.
S4.quote: I want a small, solid, reliable life, earning enough to help my parents when they're older.
fieldNote: Her hopes are modest and **concrete**: flat, team, boss.
She wants to learn tools from colleagues, not alone.
Fear of stagnation is her main worry here.

steps.text: Take a first job in a team that already uses AI tools
Learn the team's AI tool from a patient colleague
Save for a flat deposit by age 27

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because I'm the slowest to pick things up and I'd have no time. What would help is steady, practical training near home, taught in person, and employers who still take on a few beginners.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I know I sound stubborn. I'm not against change, I'm against change that arrives with a manual and no person. Give me one patient teacher and I'll keep up.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change, I'm against change that arrives with a manual and no person.
portrait: Jade is 23, a marketing graduate in Hallbeck living with her parents, grandfather and dog Biscuit, with no offer yet.
She avoids AI tools and likes **routine**: three applications a day, a walk every morning.
Her centre views make her pragmatic and cautious, and she distrusts big claims.
In the fast scenarios her fear grows because she is **slow to learn** tools and sees no time to catch up.
She learns best with a patient person beside her and wants a small, **reliable life**.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most, since she is slowest to pick things up and would have no time.
whatWouldHelp: Employers who still take on a few beginners.
